title: The Listening Well
premise: Folklorist Sebastian Almeida returns to the village of Hollowmere to record its songs, only to find the villagers refuse to sing any of them twice—and her childhood imaginary friend, Wren, waiting on her porch exactly as she left him twenty years ago. As she digs into the village's archives, she learns the 'Listening Well' at the town's heart keeps something fed through song, and that every villager who once sang with her as a child has since gone silent, or gone missing. To survive, Sebastian must learn the song's forbidden last verse without ever singing it aloud—but Wren, unchanged and increasingly desperate not to be forgotten again, needs her voice. In the end, Sebastian chooses truth over belonging: she records the final verse and plays it back into the well, trading her own memory of childhood for the village's release, and walks out of Hollowmere unable to remember why she came.
about_author: Oscar Ashgrove is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing oral histories in remote coastal villages before turning to fiction. Their work blends field-recording aesthetics with folk horror, exploring what communities bury to keep singing.

chapters.title: The House That Counts Its Doors
chapters.summary: Sebastian arrives in Hollowmere to record its songs, settling into her late grandmother's cottage where she compulsively counts doors each night. POV: Sebastian. Emotional beat: uneasy homecoming—the village feels familiar in ways that frighten her, and the first recorded song plays back with an extra voice on it.

chapters.title: Wren on the Porch
chapters.summary: Sebastian finds Wren—her childhood imaginary friend—waiting on the porch, unchanged after twenty years, greeting her like no time has passed. POV: Sebastian. Emotional beat: vertiginous joy curdling into dread; he knows things about the village's silences that no imaginary friend should.

chapters.title: No One Sings It Twice
chapters.summary: Sebastian interviews villagers who each sing one verse of the Well Song but flatly refuse to repeat it; old Marta warns her that repetition is an invitation. POV: Sebastian. Emotional beat: mounting isolation as warmth turns to stonewalling, revealing the village is protecting her—or protecting itself from her.

chapters.title: The Verse That Wasn't Recorded
chapters.summary: Reviewing her grandmother's old field tapes, Sebastian discovers every recording skips at the same moment—the fourth verse—replaced by thirty seconds of well water. POV: Sebastian, with tape-transcript interludes. Emotional beat: scholarly obsession igniting; the gap in the archive becomes a wound she must fill.

chapters.title: Children Who Sang Together
chapters.summary: Sebastian uncovers a 1998 photo of six children singing at the well—herself among them—and learns three are dead and two haven't spoken since. POV: Sebastian. Emotional beat: grief and guilt; Wren appears beside her in the photo, though she remembers him as invisible.

chapters.title: What the Well Keeps
chapters.summary: Marta finally explains: the Well listens, and it keeps what it hears—a voice, a memory, a child. The village sings once a year to feed it and stay forgotten by it. POV: alternating Sebastian and Marta's testimony. Emotional beat: horror reframed as maintenance; belonging bought with deliberate forgetting.

chapters.title: The Friend Who Wouldn't Fade
chapters.summary: Wren grows desperate as Sebastian nears the truth, begging her to sing with him like they used to; when she refuses, doors in the cottage begin multiplying overnight. POV: Sebastian. Emotional beat: betrayal—her oldest companion may be the Well's keeper, or its loneliest prisoner.

chapters.title: Down Where the Water Listens
chapters.summary: Sebastian descends into the well shaft and finds the missing singers preserved mid-song, mouths open, eyes tracking her—including the woman she might have become. POV: Sebastian. Emotional beat: terror and terrible recognition; the Well doesn't kill, it collects, and it has been saving her a place.

chapters.title: The Last Verse
chapters.summary: Climax. On the night of the annual singing, Sebastian learns the final verse from the collected voices themselves and must record it without singing along while Wren weeps and the whole village hums around her. POV: Sebastian. Emotional beat: agonizing choice between loyalty to Wren and truth; she presses record and stays silent.

chapters.title: A Woman Who Can't Remember Why She Came
chapters.summary: Sebastian plays the recording into the Well; the collected voices disperse, Wren thanks her and dissolves, and the village wakes free—but Sebastian's childhood memories drain away with them. POV: Sebastian, then a detached third person. Emotional beat: bittersweet resolution; she leaves Hollowmere whole yet hollowed, keeping only a tape she cannot explain.
